sections.b: Four chapters, 104 verses: thanks and news (1:1-26), the call to live as citizens worthy of the good news and the Christ hymn (1:27-2:18), Timothy and Epaphroditus (2:19-30), the warning and Paul's story (3), and the closing appeals and thanks (4). The 'think' verb, joy and partnership run through all four chapters.

common: Philippians is a letter of joy written from prison.
uncommon: Philippians joins two or three letters Paul wrote at different times.

sections.b: The church at Philippi was Paul's partner 'from the first day' (Philippians 1:5), sending help to him in Thessalonica and later in prison (Philippians 4:15-18). Its people had seen Paul beaten in their city (Philippians 1:30; Acts 16:22-24). Paul's language of citizenship (Philippians 1:27; 3:20) was written for a Roman colony.

Paul introduces the hymn with 'Think this way among yourselves' (Philippians 2:5) and follows it with 'work out your own salvation' (Philippians 2:12). Its words return in his own story: he counts his status as loss (Philippians 3:7-8), takes on the form of Christ's death (Philippians 3:10), and expects Christ to refashion the body 'to share the form of his body of glory' (Philippians 3:21). The church's quarrels (Philippians 4:2) are the setting that makes the hymn practical.

common: Christ emptied himself by taking a slave's form and becoming human, without ceasing to be God.
uncommon: The hymn contrasts Jesus with Adam and does not speak of his existence before birth.

claude.title: Claude's theory: the 'form' words make chapter 3 a retelling of the hymn
claude.body: See the spec box on the Philippians book page: the words count, form, found, low, refashion and Lord tie Paul's own story in chapter 3 to the hymn in chapter 2, which may argue for the letter's unity. This is my own suggestion, built on links many commentators have noticed.

sections.b: Paul prays 'with joy' (Philippians 1:4), rejoices that Christ is announced even by rivals (Philippians 1:18), asks the church to 'make my joy full' by unity (Philippians 2:2), rejoices even if poured out as a drink offering (Philippians 2:17-18), and commands 'Rejoice in the Lord at all times' (Philippians 4:4). The Philippians themselves are 'my joy and my victory wreath' (Philippians 4:1).

sections.h: Paul in prison, and his Jewish record
sections.b: Philippians gives Paul's own list of his Jewish credentials: circumcised on the eighth day, of Israel and the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew whose parents were Hebrews, a Pharisee, a zealous persecutor of the church, blameless in the righteousness the law speaks of (Philippians 3:5-6). It also shows him in chains, uncertain of the verdict, yet ready for life or death (Philippians 1:20-24). Where he was held, Rome, Ephesus or Caesarea, is debated.

Timothy is co-sender of the letter (Philippians 1:1). Paul praises him as the one who 'shares my heart' and will 'honestly worry about your affairs', who served with him 'like a child beside his father', and plans to send him to Philippi soon (Philippians 2:19-23).

Philippians 1:1 greets the church 'with overseers and deacons', plural overseers in one city. Readers have seen in it the roots of the later order of bishops, priests and deacons, or the single office of elder-overseer that Acts 20:17, 28 also suggests. See the card on Philippians 1.

Philippians 1:1 is one of the earliest places where diakonoi are named beside overseers as a group in a church. Calvin took them to be stewards of the church's alms; their exact duties are not described.

sections.h: To leave and be with Christ
sections.b: Paul longs 'to leave and be with Christ', which is 'much, much better' (Philippians 1:23), while placing his main hope in the resurrection at Christ's coming (Philippians 3:20-21). The Westminster Confession cites the verse for the soul's immediate entry into heaven; the Catholic Catechism speaks of life in heaven as being 'with Christ' and of purification after death for some. See the card on Philippians 1.

sections.h: The form of God and equality with God
sections.b: The hymn says Christ was 'in the form of God' and did not count 'equality with God' as something to exploit (Philippians 2:6), and that God gave him the name above every name (Philippians 2:9-11). It was central in the debates of the fourth century: Chrysostom used it against the Arians and the followers of Paul of Samosata.

Isaiah 45:23 has the LORD, who says 'there is no one else', swear that every knee will bend to him. Philippians 2:10-11 applies the oath to Jesus and ends 'for the glory of God the Father', so the confession of Jesus as Lord stays inside the worship of the one God.

God gives the exalted Jesus 'the name / that is above every name' (Philippians 2:9), most likely 'Lord', the Greek Bible's word for the divine name, so that every tongue confesses 'Jesus Christ is Lord' (Philippians 2:11).

sections.h: The slave's form and Isaiah's servant
sections.b: Many readers hear Isaiah's servant in Philippians 2:7-9: the servant who 'emptied out his life to the point of death' (Isaiah 53:12) and who would be 'he will be high and lifted up, / and very exalted' (Isaiah 52:13). Paul also borrows the servant's words 'worked hard for nothing' (Isaiah 49:4) in Philippians 2:16.

The hymn's lowest point is 'death on a cross' (Philippians 2:8), the Roman death for slaves and rebels, and the line may be Paul's own addition to an earlier hymn. Paul later weeps over 'enemies of Christ's cross' (Philippians 3:18).

Paul gives up 'a righteousness of my own, the kind that comes from the law' for 'the righteousness that is from God and is based on faith' (Philippians 3:9). The Reformation churches read it as righteousness counted to the believer; Catholic teaching as God's gift that makes the believer truly righteous; the New Perspective as covenant status opened to Gentiles in Christ. See the card on Philippians 3.

Philippians 3:9 has 'through faith of Christ' followed by 'based on faith'. The Plain reads 'faith in Christ', as at Romans 3:22 and Galatians 2:16; on the subjective reading the verse names Christ's faithfulness and then the believer's faith. Both sides cite the verse.

Paul calls himself 'blameless' in the righteousness the law speaks of (Philippians 3:6) and gives up 'a righteousness of my own' (Philippians 3:9). Readers after Krister Stendahl see no guilty conscience here; New Perspective readers take 'my own righteousness' as covenant status rather than earned merit.

Paul warns against 'the mutilation', a mocking pun on circumcision, and claims 'We are the circumcision' for those who worship by the Spirit of God (Philippians 3:2-3), while counting his own eighth-day circumcision as real (Philippians 3:5). The issue is whether Gentile believers must be circumcised.

'Look out for the dogs' (Philippians 3:2) has been turned against Jews. John Chrysostom, preaching on the verse, called the dogs Jews who 'preached both Christianity and Judaism at the same time' and said that 'once the Gentiles were called dogs, but now the Jews' (Homily 10 on Philippians). The most common modern reading is that Paul means Jewish-Christian teachers who would require circumcision of Gentile believers; others think of local Jews or other groups. Paul lists his own Jewish identity with pride (Philippians 3:5). The letter's echo of Deuteronomy 32:5, 'a warped and twisted generation' (Philippians 2:15), describes the church's mostly Gentile neighbors.

Philippians 3:2 warns against 'the dogs', 'the bad workers' and 'the mutilation', most likely teachers like the agitators in Galatia who required circumcision of Gentile believers. Whether they had reached Philippi is uncertain.

sections.h: 'When it came to the law, I was a Pharisee'
sections.b: Paul names his Pharisee past among his credentials (Philippians 3:5), as he does in Acts 23:6 and 26:5, and counts it, with his other advantages, as loss compared with knowing Christ.

Paul denies he has 'already been made perfect' (Philippians 3:12) yet calls the mature 'perfect' (Philippians 3:15). Wesley's sermon 'Christian Perfection' takes 3:12 as its text; the Westminster Confession calls sanctification 'imperfect in this life'. See the card on Philippians 3.

sections.h: God at work, and working out salvation
sections.b: 'With fear and trembling, work out your own salvation. For the one at work in you is God' (Philippians 2:12-13). Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Reformed and Methodist teachers all cite these verses, and differ on how grace and the human will work together. See the card on Philippians 2.

'Salvation' in Philippians can be release or vindication at Paul's trial (Philippians 1:19, quoting Job 13:16), the end God promises his people (Philippians 1:28), and what believers 'work out' as God works in them (Philippians 2:12-13). From heaven they await 'a Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ' (Philippians 3:20).

sections.h: The body of our low state
sections.b: Christ 'will refashion the body we have in our low state, to share the form of his body of glory' (Philippians 3:21): the same body changed, by the power that puts all things under him. 1 Corinthians 15:42-53 says the same at length.

Paul calls Euodia and Syntyche women who 'fought at my side in spreading the good news', with Clement and his other fellow workers (Philippians 4:2-3). Chrysostom thought they seemed to be 'the chief of the Church which was there'. The church itself began with Lydia and the women at the place of prayer (Acts 16:13-15).

'You have been given this as a gift, on Christ's behalf: not only believing in him, but suffering for his sake too' (Philippians 1:29). Paul wants to share Christ's sufferings, 'taking on the form of his death' (Philippians 3:10), and writes of joy from prison.

sections.h: Lord and Savior in a Roman colony
sections.b: In a colony where the emperor could be called 'lord' (compare Acts 25:26), the hymn's 'Jesus Christ is Lord' (Philippians 2:11) and the church's wait for 'a Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ' from heaven (Philippians 3:20) carried a local edge. Paul even sends greetings from Caesar's household (Philippians 4:22).

'The whole praetorium' (Philippians 1:13) and 'Caesar's household' (Philippians 4:22) fit a Roman imprisonment, the traditional view, though both terms were used in the provinces too. Acts ends with Paul under guard in Rome (Acts 28:16, 30-31).

Paul pictures his possible death as a drink offering poured over the sacrifice of the Philippians' faith (Philippians 2:17), and their gift as 'a soothing smell, a sacrifice that God accepts' (Philippians 4:18), the language of Numbers 15 and Genesis 8:21.

sections.h: Names in the book of life
sections.b: Paul says his co-workers' 'names are in the book of life' (Philippians 4:3), the register of God's people found from Exodus 32:32 to Revelation 3:5, fitting for a church of citizens.

The Philippians' gifts to Paul (Philippians 4:10-18) are described in business words (an account, giving and receiving, paid in full) and temple words (a sacrifice). Paul has learned to be content with plenty or little (Philippians 4:11-12), and promises that God will fill their every need (Philippians 4:19).

sections.h: Slaves of Christ, and a slave's form
sections.b: Paul and Timothy call themselves 'slaves of Christ Jesus' (Philippians 1:1), and the hymn says Christ took 'a slave's form' (Philippians 2:7), the lowest status in a Roman colony. Paul uses slave status as a picture, of belonging wholly to Christ and of Christ's self-lowering, without commenting on slavery as an institution in this letter.
Philippians speaks of 'the day of Christ Jesus' (Philippians 1:6) and 'the day of Christ' (Philippians 1:10; 2:16), giving the prophets' day of the LORD the name of Christ.

Philippians is in Papyrus 46, an early codex of Paul's letters. Its notable differences between editions include the order of 1:16-17 (the oldest manuscripts and modern Bibles give the 'love' sentence first; the Byzantine text and the KJV, whose numbering this site follows, give the 'selfish ambition' sentence first), the clause 'or already justified' that P46 adds at 3:12, 'Christ' added at 4:13, and the longer ending of 3:16 in the Byzantine text. See the variant entries.
